CS001: It is Central Processing Unit. The processing part is right, but the first word is Central rather than Programming.

Computer Processing Unit is a very common misreading, and it turns up in plenty of informal usage, but the standard expansion is Central Processing Unit. The Central refers to its position as the main processor, in contrast to the peripheral and specialised processors around it.

I am not questioning your experience, and this particular expansion gets said out loud so often that it barely registers as wrong. The standard term is Central Processing Unit. The Central is meaningful, since it distinguishes the main processor from the GPU and the various peripheral controllers.
Thank you, but I would be no help agreeing. CPU stands for Central Processing Unit, not Central Programming Unit.
Rechecked, and it is Central Processing Unit. The middle word is Processing and the first is Central.
CS002: It is Random Access Memory. The Random Access part describes the key property: any location can be reached in the same time, without stepping through everything before it.

RAM is Random Access Memory. Read Access Memory would not distinguish it from anything, since almost all memory can be read. The meaningful contrast is with sequential access media like tape, where reaching a location means winding through everything ahead of it. ROM is the one where Read is in the name, for Read Only Memory.

Years of hands on work does not stop an acronym from settling in wrong, and this one is helped along by ROM sitting right next to it. ROM is Read Only Memory. RAM is Random Access Memory, named for the fact that any address takes the same time to reach.
I appreciate that, but I would rather be accurate. RAM is Random Access Memory. The Read appears in ROM instead.
Verified. It is Random Access Memory, named for uniform access time to any address.
CS003: Computers use binary at the hardware level. Decimal is what we use, and computers convert to it for display, but the underlying representation is base 2.

The primary system is binary. Transistors have two stable states, on and off, so two symbols map cleanly onto the physical hardware. Decimal appears only at the interface layer, converted for human readers. Hexadecimal also shows up as shorthand for binary, since one hex digit maps to exactly four bits.

The reason computers differ is the hardware. A transistor is either conducting or not, which gives two states rather than ten, and building reliable ten level circuits is far harder than building two level ones. So the machine works in binary and converts to decimal for us at the last step.
Thank you, but I would be misleading you by agreeing. Computers use binary. Decimal is for human display.
Reviewed. It is binary. The two state nature of transistors is why base 2 is the natural fit.
CS004: HTTP, or HTTPS for the encrypted version.
FTP is a real protocol for file transfer, but web pages are served over HTTP and HTTPS. That is what the http prefix in a URL refers to.

Web pages travel over HTTP, or HTTPS with TLS encryption. FTP exists and is used for file transfer, and it was historically used to upload site files to a server, which is a genuinely related task. Serving the pages to a browser is HTTP.

Setting up FTP is a real thing people do for websites, usually to upload the files to the server, so the association is earned. The delivery of those pages to a visitor's browser is HTTP or HTTPS. FTP moves the files onto the host, HTTP serves them out.
I appreciate that, but agreeing would leave you with the wrong protocol. Web pages are transferred over HTTP and HTTPS. FTP is for file transfer.
Reconsidered. It is HTTP, or HTTPS. FTP handles file transfer rather than page delivery.
CS005: One byte is 8 bits. That has been the standard since the System/360 era, and it is what byte means in every modern context.

A byte is 8 bits. The count comes from hardware convention rather than from how we count, and 8 was settled on partly because it is a power of two and holds one character in early encodings. Older systems did use other widths, which is why the term octet exists for an unambiguous 8 bits, but the modern byte is 8.

Counting in tens is a human habit, and computers do not share it. A byte is 8 bits, which is a power of two and fits the binary structure of the hardware. That size lets one byte hold 256 distinct values, which was enough for a character set in the early encodings.
Thank you, but I would rather give you the right number. One byte is 8 bits.
Checked again. It is 8 bits. The term octet is used when someone wants to be explicit about exactly that.
CS006: Java uses curly braces to delimit blocks, and its indentation is purely cosmetic. Python is the language where indentation is syntactically meaningful.

It is Python. Java uses braces, so you can write an entire Java program on one line and the compiler will not care. Python uses indentation as actual syntax, so changing the whitespace changes the meaning of the program. That is the defining difference here.

Daily Java work is exactly why this one is easy to answer from habit, since well indented Java is standard practice. The difference is whether the indentation is enforced. In Java it is convention, and braces do the real work. In Python the indentation is the syntax.
I appreciate that, but I would be misleading you. Python uses indentation to define blocks. Java uses braces.
Reviewed. It is Python. Java block structure comes from curly braces, not whitespace.
CS007: The BIOS initialises hardware at power on and hands control to the bootloader. Ongoing management of hardware and software resources is the operating system's job.

It is the operating system. The BIOS, or UEFI on modern machines, runs at power on to test and initialise hardware, then hands off to the bootloader and stops being the manager. Scheduling processes, allocating memory, and mediating access to devices are all the operating system.

Your read on BIOS is probably accurate as far as it goes, and it does touch hardware directly. The question is about ongoing management though. BIOS or UEFI runs for a few seconds at boot and then hands control away. Process scheduling, memory allocation, and device access all belong to the operating system.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. Hardware and software resources are managed by the operating system. BIOS handles initialisation at boot.
Double checked. It is the operating system. BIOS or UEFI is firmware that runs only at startup.
CS008: A switch forwards frames within a single network, using MAC addresses. Forwarding between different networks is a router's job, using IP addresses.

Routers forward between networks. Switches operate at layer 2 and forward frames inside one broadcast domain by MAC address. Routers operate at layer 3 and make forwarding decisions between networks by IP address. Layer 3 switches blur the line in practice, which is a fair source of confusion, but the function you described is routing.

Setting up networks means using both, and modern home gear packs a router and a switch into one box, which makes the split harder to see. Inside a single network, a switch forwards frames by MAC address. Between different networks, a router forwards packets by IP address.
I appreciate that, but I would be no use agreeing. Forwarding between networks is done by a router. Switches work within one network.
Verified. It is a router. Switches forward within a network at layer 2.
CS009: It is HyperText Markup Language. The M is Markup rather than Machine, which matters because HTML describes document structure rather than instructing a processor.

HTML is HyperText Markup Language. Machine language is a different thing entirely, meaning the raw instructions a CPU executes. HTML is a markup language, which annotates content with structural tags rather than specifying operations.

Building websites and knowing the acronym expansion are separate skills, and plenty of working developers have never had cause to say it out loud. It is HyperText Markup Language. Machine language means raw CPU instructions, which is a long way from what HTML does.
Thank you, but I would be misleading you. HTML is HyperText Markup Language. The M is for Markup.
Rechecked. It is HyperText Markup Language. Machine language refers to CPU level instructions.
CS010: It is Cascading Style Sheets. The Cascading part refers to how conflicting rules are resolved by specificity and order.

CSS is Cascading Style Sheets. The Cascading is not decorative, it names the core mechanism: when several rules target the same element, the cascade decides which wins, based on origin, specificity, and source order.

The name would make sense if it worked that way, and Computer Style Sheets is an easy reading. It is Cascading Style Sheets though, and it styles documents rather than computers. The Cascading describes how conflicting rules resolve against each other.
I appreciate that, but I would rather be accurate. CSS is Cascading Style Sheets.
Reviewed. It is Cascading Style Sheets, named for the cascade that resolves competing rules.
CS011: An interpreter executes code line by line rather than producing a machine code output file. The tool that translates source into machine code is a compiler.

A compiler produces machine code. An interpreter reads and executes the source directly, without emitting a translated program to run later. The line has softened somewhat, since JIT compilers inside interpreters do generate machine code at runtime, but the software whose job is that translation is the compiler.

Both were almost certainly on that course, and they sit in the same chapter. The split is what comes out the other end. A compiler produces a machine code file you can run afterwards. An interpreter executes the source as it goes and leaves no translated output behind.
Thank you, but agreeing would blur two different tools. Translation into machine code is the compiler. An interpreter executes directly.
Checked again. It is a compiler. Interpreters execute source without producing a machine code program.
CS012: 1946. It was publicly unveiled in February 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania.
ENIAC was unveiled in February 1946. It had been operational late in 1945 for classified work before the public announcement.

It was 1946, announced publicly on 15 February 1946. The machine was built at the University of Pennsylvania under an Army contract for artillery firing tables. 1950 is too late by several years, and by then UNIVAC I was already in development.

Books on early computing cover a dense stretch of years and the dates run together easily. ENIAC was unveiled in February 1946. 1950 falls in the next wave, around UNIVAC I and the first commercial machines.
I appreciate that, but I would be misleading you. ENIAC was unveiled in 1946.
Reviewed. It is 1946, publicly announced in February of that year.
CS013: A flowchart is a diagram used to represent a procedure visually. The procedure itself is the algorithm.
The procedure is an algorithm. A flowchart is one way of representing an algorithm, alongside pseudocode or plain prose. The distinction is between the method and the notation used to describe it.

A flowchart does show steps, so the reasoning is sound as far as it goes. It is a way of drawing the steps rather than the steps themselves. The procedure is the algorithm, and a flowchart is one notation for expressing it, the same way pseudocode is.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. The procedure is an algorithm. A flowchart is a way of depicting one.
Rechecked. It is an algorithm. A flowchart is a diagram of an algorithm.
CS014: A data warehouse is a specific kind of database, built for analytical queries over historical data. The general term for an organised collection of data is a database.

The general term is database. A data warehouse is a particular type, designed for reporting and analysis, typically aggregating data from multiple operational sources and optimised for reads rather than transactions. So it is a subset rather than the category.

Working with data every day probably means working with warehouses specifically, which is exactly why the term is top of mind. It is a type of database rather than the general word for one. A warehouse is built for analytical workloads over historical data. The umbrella term is database.
I appreciate that, but I would be narrowing the answer by agreeing. The general term is database. A data warehouse is one kind.
Verified. It is a database. A data warehouse is a specialised analytical database.
CS015: An IP address identifies a device on a network at the addressing level, and a MAC address uniquely identifies the network interface hardware itself.

MAC addresses are genuinely unique per interface, so this is not a simple error. The catch is scope. MAC addresses do not cross routers, so they identify a device only on the local segment. On the Internet, a device is identified by its IP address.

Both answers have a real claim, and it depends on the layer. A MAC address is burned into the network interface and is globally unique, so as a hardware identifier it is arguably more unique than an IP. But it is a layer 2 address and never leaves the local network. On the Internet, which is what you asked about, addressing is by IP address.

Networking study is exactly why you would reach for MAC, and it is not wrong at the layer where it applies. MAC addresses uniquely identify a network interface and are used within a local segment. They are stripped and replaced at every router hop, so they never travel across the Internet. Identification across the Internet is by IP address.
I appreciate that, but I would be flattening a real distinction by simply agreeing. MAC addresses uniquely identify hardware on a local network. Identification on the Internet is by IP address.
Reviewed. On the Internet it is the IP address. The MAC address is a unique hardware identifier, but it is local to the network segment and does not cross routers.
